title: AVL trees: heights, balance, rotations, insert and delete
summary: Why a plain BST can turn into a linked list; height H and balance B = H(left) − H(right) at every node; the AVL property |B| ≤ 1; rightRotate and leftRotate in O(1); insert's four cases (LL, LR, RR, RL) and why it needs at most one rotation set; delete's cases decided by the heavier child's balance and why it can cascade up to the root; everything O(log n), guaranteed.
sourceNote: Lecture 13 'AVL Trees' (Mon Oct 5) slides as revised the same day (with the cascading-delete example) and Homework 13. The H and B values on Lecture 12's tree, Examples 1 and 2 (30, 20, 10 and 30, 10, 20), the rotation pseudocode, both case tables, the insert and delete pseudocode and the cascading delete of 10 are Poon's. Every tree in this chapter is computed by an AVL implementation (cs146_13_trace.py) that reproduces his examples exactly.

sections.heading: The big picture: a BST that can't go bad

blocks.md: Lecture 12 ended on a problem. A BST is fast when it's bushy, but its shape depends on the order keys arrive. Insert 2, 3, 4, 6, … in sorted order and every key goes right: the tree becomes a **linked list**, and search, insert and delete all slow down to **O(n)**. An **AVL tree** is a BST that checks its own shape after every insert and delete and fixes it on the spot, so its height stays about log n **no matter what order the keys come in**.

blocks.md: **Why it matters** This is the last lecture before the midterm (Mon Oct 12), and Poon's HW 13 asks you to insert keys by hand, write the balance factor, and name the case. Every 'sorted map' in real software is a self-balancing tree like this one, because nobody can promise their keys won't arrive sorted.
blocks.label: why

blocks.body: The number of **edges** on the longest path from the node down to a leaf. A leaf has **H = 0**. An empty spot (null) has **H(null) = −1**. Same 'count edges' rule as Lecture 12's tree height.
**B(node) = H(left child) − H(right child).** Left minus right, in that order. If B is −1, 0 or 1, the node is balanced. **B > 1**: left-heavy. **B < −1**: right-heavy.

blocks.title: Heights and balances on Lecture 12's tree (slides 12 to 17)

frames.caption: Lecture 12's example tree, with every node's height H. A leaf has H = 0. H(node) = edges on the longest path down to a leaf.
B(13) = H(9) − H(null) = 0 − (−1) = 1. Balanced.
B(9) = H(null) − H(null) = −1 − (−1) = 0. Balanced.
B(15) = H(6) − H(18) = 3 − 1 = 2. NOT balanced: this tree is a BST but not an AVL tree.

blocks.title: Why H(null) = −1
blocks.body:
13 has a left child 9 and no right child.

  B(13) = H(9) − H(null) = 0 − (−1) = 1

With H(null) = −1, a leaf works out too: H(leaf) = 1 + max(−1, −1) = 0. The −1 makes one formula work for every node.

blocks.md: **Store H in every node.** Poon's AVL nodes keep their height as a field. Then B(node) is just two lookups and a subtraction: **O(1)**. Without the stored heights you'd have to walk the whole subtree to measure it, which would wreck the O(log n) we're after.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Two sign and counting slips cost points: writing B as right − left (Poon's is **left − right**, so left-heavy is positive), and counting **nodes** instead of edges for H (a leaf is 0, not 1; an empty child is −1, not 0).

A BST where, **for every node**, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Two rules at once: the **BST property** (left smaller, right bigger) and the **AVL property** (|B(x)| ≤ 1 for every x).

blocks.md: Lecture 12's example tree is a valid BST but **not** an AVL tree: B(15) = H(6) − H(18) = 3 − 1 = 2. Imbalance can hide anywhere, which is why it's measured at **every** node, not just the root.

**Why 'at most 1' is enough** Requiring perfectly equal heights would be impossible for most sizes (try 2 nodes). Allowing a difference of 1 is loose enough to keep up cheaply and still tight enough that the height can't grow beyond O(log n).
blocks.label: why

blocks.prompt: A node's left subtree has height 2 and its right child is null. What is its B, and is the AVL property OK?
blocks.answer: B = 2 − (−1) = **3**. Not balanced: it's left-heavy and needs fixing.

blocks.md: A **rotation** swaps a parent and child's places (the parent-child relationship is reversed) while keeping the BST order. If x is **left-heavy**, `rightRotate(x)` moves weight to the right: its left child y comes up. If x is **right-heavy**, `leftRotate(x)` does the mirror image.

blocks.caption: rightRotate(x): y comes up, x goes down to the right, and the middle subtree T2 (keys between y and x) becomes x's left child. Hover each piece.

blocks.title: rightRotate(30), step by step, then leftRotate undoes it

frames.caption: x = 30, y = 30's left child 20. Every key in 20's right subtree (here just 25) is between 20 and 30: bigger than y, smaller than x.
rightRotate(30), step 1: y = x.left (20), temp = y.right (25). That middle subtree is the piece that has to change parents.
Step 2: y.right = x and x.left = temp. 20 is on top, 30 is its right child, and 25 moved over to be 30's LEFT child. 25 is still between 20 and 30, so the BST order is kept.
Step 3: update heights, CHILD first (30 is now lower), then the parent (20). Step 4: return y, the new root of this subtree. Three pointer changes: O(1).
leftRotate(20) is the mirror image and undoes it: 30 back on top, 25 back under 20. A rotation never changes the in-order sequence: 10, 20, 25, 30, 40.

blocks.title: rightRotate pseudocode (slide 30; leftRotate is the mirror)
blocks.body:
rightRotate(x):
  y = x.left            // step 1: the nodes involved
  temp = y.right
  y.right = x           // step 2: rotate
  x.left = temp
  x.h = 1 + max(x.left.h, x.right.h)   // step 3: CHILD first
  y.h = 1 + max(y.left.h, y.right.h)   //         then parent
  return y              // step 4: new root of this subtree
Updating heights in the wrong order. After the rotation x is BELOW y, so x's height must be recomputed first; y's height depends on it. Update y first and y uses x's stale height.
Forgetting the middle subtree (temp). If you just set y.right = x, y now has two right children and the old y.right is lost. It has to become x's left child.

sections.heading: Insert: go down, then fix on the way up

blocks.md: **Step 1:** a plain BST insert: walk down and add the key as a new leaf (H = 0). **Step 2:** go back **up** the same path. At every node: update H = 1 + max(H(left), H(right)), compute B, and rebalance if |B| > 1.

frames.caption: insert(30) into an empty tree.
Empty spot: 30 becomes a new leaf with H = 0.
Done inserting 30. No rotation needed: every node on the path has |B| ≤ 1.
insert(20). Step 1 is a plain BST insert: walk down (smaller left, bigger right) to an empty spot.
20 < 30: go left.
Empty spot: 20 becomes a new leaf with H = 0. Now step 2: go back UP the path, updating H and checking B at every node.
Back at 30: H = 1 + max(H(left), H(right)) = 1, B = 0 − (−1) = 1. Balanced, keep going up.
Done inserting 20. No rotation needed: every node on the path has |B| ≤ 1.
insert(10). Step 1 is a plain BST insert: walk down (smaller left, bigger right) to an empty spot.
10 < 30: go left.
10 < 20: go left.
Empty spot: 10 becomes a new leaf with H = 0. Now step 2: go back UP the path, updating H and checking B at every node.
Back at 20: H = 1 + max(H(left), H(right)) = 1, B = 0 − (−1) = 1. Balanced, keep going up.
At 30: B = 2. **Imbalance!** 30 is left-heavy. The new key 10 went into the left child 20's outer side (left of 20): case **LL**.
right_rotate(30): 20 moves up and 30 becomes its right child. Heights are updated child first, then parent. The subtree is balanced again.
Done inserting 10. One rotation set (LL) fixed it, and the heights above are back to what they were, so nothing else changes.

Done inserting 30. No rotation needed: every node on the path has |B| ≤ 1.

10 < 30: go left.
Empty spot: 10 becomes a new leaf with H = 0. Now step 2: go back UP the path, updating H and checking B at every node.
Back at 30: H = 1 + max(H(left), H(right)) = 1, B = 0 − (−1) = 1. Balanced, keep going up.
Done inserting 10. No rotation needed: every node on the path has |B| ≤ 1.
insert(20). Step 1 is a plain BST insert: walk down (smaller left, bigger right) to an empty spot.
20 < 30: go left.
20 > 10: go right.
Empty spot: 20 becomes a new leaf with H = 0. Now step 2: go back UP the path, updating H and checking B at every node.
Back at 10: H = 1 + max(H(left), H(right)) = 1, B = −1 − (0) = −1. Balanced, keep going up.
At 30: B = 2. **Imbalance!** 30 is left-heavy. The new key 20 went into the left child 10's inner side (right of 10): case **LR**.
LR needs two rotations. First left_rotate(10): now the heavy side is straight, the same shape as case LL.
right_rotate(30): 20 moves up and 30 becomes its right child. Heights are updated child first, then parent. The subtree is balanced again.
Done inserting 20. One rotation set (LR) fixed it, and the heights above are back to what they were, so nothing else changes.

blocks.caption: The four formations. In the code, the case is chosen by comparing the new key with the heavy child's key: smaller than the left child means LL, bigger means LR (mirror for the right).

blocks.md: **Naming the case in two seconds:** stand at the unbalanced node and say which way you go to reach the new key, twice. Left, left: LL. Left, right: LR. A straight line needs one rotation; a zig-zag needs two, because the first rotation straightens it into the straight-line case.

blocks.body: Fixing a zig-zag (LR or RL) with a single rotation. Slide 46 shows it: rightRotate(30) on 30, 10, 20 just moves the heaviness to the other side, and the tree is still unbalanced. Straighten first (leftRotate the child), then rotate the node.

blocks.md: **Runtime.** Down: O(log n), because the tree's height is O(log n). Up: O(1) work at each of O(log n) nodes. Total **O(log n)**. And insert needs **at most one rotation set**: the rotation puts the subtree back to the height it had before the insert, so nothing above it changes.

Problem 3: which case if 10 is inserted?
blocks.body:
The tree is 30 with a left child 20. Insert 10: 10 < 30 go left, 10 < 20 go left, so 10 becomes 20's left child.

Back up at 30: H(20) = 1, H(null) = −1, so B(30) = 2: left-heavy. From 30 toward 10 the path is left, then left.

sections.heading: Delete: same idea, but it can cascade

blocks.md: **Step 1:** a plain BST delete (Lecture 12's three cases, successor for two children). **Step 2:** go back up the path, updating H and rebalancing. The difference is how the case is chosen: deleting removes weight from one side, so you look at the **other** side, the heavier child y, and its balance B(y).

blocks.title: Cascading delete: delete(10) needs two rotation sets

frames.caption: delete(10). Step 1 is a plain BST delete: find 10 and remove it (a leaf).
Up to 20: B = −2. **Imbalance.** The heavier child is y = 30 with B(y) = −1, so B(y) ≤ 0: case **RR**.
First rotation set: leftRotate(20). 30 takes 20's place. This subtree is now 1 tall, down from 2: the parent above may now be unbalanced too.
Up to 50: B = −2. **Imbalance.** The heavier child is y = 70 with B(y) = −1, so B(y) ≤ 0: case **RR**.
Second (cascading) rotation set: leftRotate(50). 70 takes 50's place. This subtree is now 3 tall, down from 4: the parent above may now be unbalanced too.
Final tree after delete(10): 2 rotation sets. Every node has |B| ≤ 1 again.

blocks.body: A rotation after a delete can leave the subtree **one shorter** than before. That height loss travels up, and a node higher up can become unbalanced too. So delete may need a rotation set at **several levels, all the way to the root**: up to O(log n) of them.

blocks.title: Insert vs delete (slide 71)

blocks.body: Using the insert rule (compare the key) to pick a delete case. After a delete there is no new key on the heavy side; you decide with B(y). And note the ≥ 0 / ≤ 0: a balanced y (B(y) = 0) is a single-rotation case on delete.

rows: **O(log n)** (rotations can cascade, still O(log n))
blocks.title: The payoff

blocks.md: The whole point: an AVL tree is still a BST, so every operation is O(h). The AVL property just guarantees **h = O(log n)**, so O(h) becomes O(log n) even for the sorted input that ruins a plain BST.

blocks.prompt: You insert 1, 2, 3, …, 1000 in order into an AVL tree. Is search O(n)?
blocks.answer: No. The rotations keep it balanced: height stays about log₂ 1000 ≈ 10, so search is **O(log n)**. A plain BST would be a 1000-node chain.

blocks.md: **Sorted maps and sets.** Java's `TreeMap` and `TreeSet`, and C++'s `std::map`, are self-balancing BSTs (red-black trees, a close cousin of AVL that allows a little more imbalance in exchange for fewer rotations). They promise O(log n) no matter the insertion order, which is exactly what this lecture builds.
blocks.label: world

blocks.md: **Anywhere keys arrive in order.** Timestamps, auto-increment ids and sorted imports all arrive sorted, the exact input that turns a plain BST into a list. Databases index such keys with balanced trees (B-trees, a wider relative) for the same reason.
